items.stem: Explain the process of formation of ‘United Kingdom of Great Britain’.
items.answer: There was no British nation before the eighteenth century. The people of the British Isles identified themselves primarily as English, Welsh, Scot or Irish, each group with its own cultural and political traditions. The British nation-state was therefore not the product of a sudden upheaval or revolution but of a long-drawn-out process. As the English nation grew steadily in wealth and power it was able to extend its influence over the other nations of the islands, and the English parliament became the instrument through which a nation-state with England at its centre was forged. The Act of Union of 1707 between England and Scotland created the ‘United Kingdom of Great Britain’, and in 1801 Ireland was forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom. A new ‘British nation’ was then forged through the propagation of a dominant English culture, its symbols being the English language, the Union Jack and the national anthem, while the older nations survived only as subordinate partners.

items.stem: How did the ideology of ‘liberalism’ affect the Europe in early nineteenth century? Explain.
items.answer: The term liberalism derives from the Latin root liber, meaning free, and in early nineteenth-century Europe it stood for a cluster of political and economic ideas. Politically it meant freedom of the individual and equality of all before the law, the end of autocracy and clerical privilege, and government by a constitution and an elected parliament rather than by an absolute monarch. Its idea of equality was, however, limited: liberals opposed universal adult franchise, and the right to vote was confined to propertied men, with women excluded altogether. Liberalism also stressed the inviolability of private property. In the economic sphere it stood for freedom of markets and the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital, a demand that led directly to the customs union or Zollverein. Liberalism thus gave the middle classes of Europe a programme that combined constitutional government with economic freedom.

items.stem: Why was the period of 1848 considered as phase of the revolution of the Liberals in Europe?
items.answer: The events of February 1848 in France brought about the abdication of the monarch and the proclamation of a republic based on universal male suffrage. In other parts of Europe where independent nation-states did not yet exist — Germany, Italy, Poland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire — men and women of the liberal middle classes combined their demand for constitutionalism with the demand for national unification. They used the growing popular unrest to press for a nation-state founded on parliamentary principles: a constitution, freedom of the press and freedom of association. In the German regions a large number of political associations, whose members were middle-class professionals, businessmen and prosperous artisans, came together at Frankfurt and voted for an all-German National Assembly. The movement failed because the opposition of the aristocracy and the military grew stronger while the assembly, dominated by the middle classes, resisted the demands of workers and artisans and so lost their support; troops were called in and the assembly was forced to disband. The issue of political rights for women also remained unresolved even though women had formed their own political associations, founded newspapers and taken part in meetings and demonstrations. Because the initiative, the demands and the leadership all came from the liberal middle classes, 1848 is called the revolution of the liberals.

items.stem: “The first clear expression of nationalism came with the ‘French Revolution’ in 1789.” Examine the statement.
items.answer: The statement is true. Till 1789 France was a full-fledged territorial state under an absolute monarch, and the political and constitutional changes brought by the French Revolution transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to the body of French citizens. The revolution proclaimed that it was the people who would henceforth constitute the nation and shape its destiny. From the beginning the revolutionaries introduced measures and practices that created a sense of collective identity: a new tri-colour flag replaced the royal standard, the Estates General was elected by the body of active citizens and renamed the National Assembly, new hymns were composed, oaths taken and martyrs commemorated in the name of the nation, a centralised system of administration with uniform laws was framed, internal customs duties and dues were abolished, and a uniform system of weights and measures was adopted. Regional dialects were discouraged and French, as spoken and written in Paris, became the common language of the nation. The revolutionaries further declared that they would help other peoples of Europe to become nations; students and educated middle classes set up Jacobin clubs, and French armies moved into Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and much of Italy in the 1790s. With the outbreak of the revolutionary wars, nationalism spread across Europe.

items.stem: How did a wave of economic nationalism strengthen the wider nationalist sentiment growing in Europe? Explain.
items.answer: In the first half of the nineteenth century Napoleon’s administrative measures had created out of countless small principalities a confederation of thirty-nine German states. Each of these possessed its own currency and its own weights and measures, and duties were often levied according to the weight or measurement of the goods, so that a merchant moving goods across the region had to deal with a bewildering succession of tariffs and standards. The new commercial classes viewed these conditions as obstacles to economic exchange and growth. As a result the Zollverein, a customs union, was formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia and was joined by most of the German states. It abolished tariff barriers and created a unified economic territory allowing the unhindered movement of goods, people and capital, and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two. It created national unity in economic matters at a time when Germany was politically divided, and accustomed the German states to co-operating with one another without Austria, which was not a member. This was the beginning of German unity: economic nationalism strengthened the wider nationalist sentiment growing among Germans and in Europe generally.

items.stem: “The idealistic liberal-democratic sentiment of nationalism in the first half of the 19th century became a narrow creed with limited ends.” Examine the statement.
items.answer: In the last quarter of the nineteenth century nationalism changed its character. It no longer retained the idealistic liberal-democratic sentiment of the first half of the century but became a narrow creed with limited ends, and nationalist groups became increasingly intolerant of each other and ever ready to go to war. The clearest example of this narrow creed was the Balkans. A large part of the Balkans was under the control of the Ottoman Empire, and with the weakening and disintegration of that empire nationalist tensions emerged in the area as its European subject nationalities broke away and declared independence. The people of the Balkans argued that they had once been independent before foreign powers controlled them, so their object was to regain their lost independence, and each claimed territory that another also claimed. The major European powers, jealous of one another’s influence over the region, intervened in turn. The result was that the rivalries of the European powers and among the Balkan states themselves led to a series of wars in the region and finally to the First World War.

items.stem: “The Habsburg Empire that ruled over Austria-Hungary, was a patchwork of many different regions and people.” Justify the statement with suitable examples.
items.answer: In the mid-eighteenth century there were no ‘nation-states’ in Europe as we know them today. Germany, Italy and Switzerland were divided into kingdoms, duchies and cantons whose rulers held autonomous territories, and Eastern and Central Europe lay under autocratic monarchies within whose territories lived very diverse peoples. These people did not see themselves as sharing a collective identity or a common culture: different languages were spoken and people belonged to different ethnic groups. The Habsburg Empire that ruled over Austria-Hungary is the clearest example of such a patchwork. It included the Alpine regions — the Tyrol, Austria and the Sudetenland — as well as Bohemia, where the aristocracy was predominantly German-speaking. It also included the Italian-speaking provinces of Lombardy and Venetia. In Hungary half the population spoke Magyar while the other half spoke a variety of local dialects, and in Galicia the aristocracy spoke Polish. Besides these dominant groups there lived within the boundaries of the empire a mass of subject peasant peoples — Bohemians and Slovaks to the north, Slovenes in Carniola, Croats to the south and Roumans to the east in Transylvania. Such differences did not easily promote a sense of political unity, and the only tie binding these diverse groups together was a common allegiance to the emperor.

items.stem: How did nationalism develop through culture in Europe? Explain. or Describe the cultural process through which nationalism captured people’s imagination.
items.answer: Culture played an important role in creating the idea of the nation in Europe. Art and poetry, stories and music helped shape and express nationalist feeling. Romanticism, a cultural movement, sought to develop a particular form of nationalist sentiment by criticising the glorification of reason and science and focusing instead on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings, so as to create a sense of a shared collective heritage as the basis of a nation; Eugene Delacroix’s ‘The Massacre at Chios’, for example, appealed to the emotions aroused by the Greek struggle. The German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder claimed that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people — das Volk — through their folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances, which expressed the true spirit of the nation. Karol Kurpinski celebrated the national struggle through his operas and folk dances. Allegories such as Marianne and Germania gave the nation a concrete visual form. The emphasis on vernacular language and the collection of local folklore recovered an ancient national spirit and carried the nationalist message to large audiences who were mostly illiterate. Culture thus strengthened nationalist feelings across Europe.

items.stem: How did a wave of economic nationalism strengthen the wider nationalist sentiment growing in Europe? Explain.
items.answer: The economic condition of the German-speaking regions in the first half of the nineteenth century made economic unity a nationalist demand. Napoleon’s administrative measures had created, out of countless small principalities, a confederation of thirty-nine states. Each possessed its own currency, weights and measures, and duties were often levied according to the weight or measurement of the goods, so that trade across the region was obstructed at every border. The new commercial classes viewed these conditions as obstacles to economic exchange and growth. Accordingly the Zollverein, a customs union, was formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia and was joined by most of the German states. It created a unified economic territory allowing the unhindered movement of goods, people and capital, and it created national unity in economic matters at a time when Germany was politically divided. It accustomed the German states to co-operating with one another without Austria, which never became a member, and it was thus the beginning of German unity. In this way economic nationalism strengthened the wider nationalist sentiments among Germans and in Europe as a whole.

items.stem: Why was the Balkans the most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871? Explain any four reasons? or Why did nationalist tension emerge in the Balkans? Explain any four reasons.
items.answer: The Balkans became the most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871 for the following reasons. First, the Balkans was a region of great geographical and ethnic variation, comprising modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, whose inhabitants were broadly known as Slavs. Second, a large part of the Balkans was under the control of the Ottoman Empire, and the spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism in the region, together with the disintegration of that empire, made the area very explosive. Third, as the different Slavic nationalities struggled to define their identity and win independence, each claimed on the basis of a supposed past history that it had once been independent but had later been subjugated by foreign powers, so the Balkan area became one of intense conflict and the states were jealous of one another, each hoping to gain more territory at the expense of its neighbours. Fourth, the Balkans also became an arena of big-power rivalry: Russia, Germany, England and Austria-Hungary each sought to counter the hold of the others over the region. These rivalries led to a series of wars in the region and eventually to the First World War.

items.stem: Explain any five social and administrative reforms introduced by Napoleon in the regions under his control.
items.answer: Napoleon abolished the surviving feudal order in the territories he controlled and reformed their social and administrative life. First, he made the administration rational and efficient, replacing the confusing patchwork of local authorities with a uniform system. Second, the Civil Code of 1804, known as the Napoleonic Code, did away with all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property. Third, he simplified administrative divisions and abolished the arbitrary powers of local rulers. Fourth, in the countryside he abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues. Fifth, in the towns he removed guild restrictions on craftsmen and workers. He also improved transport and communication systems, and introduced a common national currency together with uniform weights and measures across the regions. Merchants and small-scale producers in particular welcomed these measures, which made movement and exchange of goods easier.

items.stem: How was the history of the development of nationalism in England different from the rest of Europe?
items.answer: The pattern of nationalism in England was different in the following ways. The emergence of nationalism there was not the result of a sudden upheaval, revolution or uprising as it was elsewhere in Europe. There was no British nation prior to the eighteenth century; the islands were inhabited by different ethnic groups — English, Welsh, Scots and Irish — each with its own cultural and political traditions. Of these the English group steadily grew in power, wealth and importance and extended its influence over the others. In 1688, through a bloodless revolution, the English parliament seized power from the monarchy and became the instrument that set up a nation-state with England at its centre. By the Act of Union of 1707 Scotland was incorporated into the United Kingdom, and although the Irish Catholics were against a union with England, Ireland was forcibly incorporated in 1801. It was therefore parliamentary action rather than revolution or war that was the instrument through which the United Kingdom was forged into a strong nation-state.

items.stem: What were the similarities between the process of unification of Germany and Italy? Write in detail.
items.answer: The unification of Germany and of Italy resembled each other in several ways. Both countries were divided into a large number of small states which lacked unity. In both, Napoleon Bonaparte indirectly encouraged unification and nationalist feeling by sweeping away the old order. In both, the Vienna Congress of 1815 again divided the countries into smaller states and restored conservative rule. Both suffered under the reactionary policies of Austria and had to fight against Austria to achieve unity. In both, the efforts of revolutionaries in 1830 and 1848 failed, and the unifications were finally accomplished not by the people but by the rulers and their chief ministers — Bismarck in Prussia and Cavour in Piedmont-Sardinia — through diplomacy and war. In both cases the new states became monarchies rather than republics after liberation and unification, and although democratic and revolutionary leaders and ordinary people played a vital part, they remained loyal to their respective kings.
items.ocr: The question compares Germany and Italy; tagged to the Italy concept because the German unification process is separately tagged at question 163.

items.stem: Discuss the general characteristics of the nationalist movement in Poland.
items.answer: Poland in the seventeenth century was a fairly large state, but her neighbours Russia, Austria and Prussia were hostile and fought long and bloody wars with her. Poland was partitioned three times — in 1772, 1793 and 1795 — and by 1795 she had ceased to exist as an independent country. Under Czar Nicholas I, a harsh autocrat, the patriotic Poles were mercilessly suppressed, and although Alexander I had granted Poland a constitution, he gave up his liberalism and became a reactionary under the influence of Metternich of Austria. The Polish revolutionaries within Russia began an armed movement, but Nicholas I crushed the revolt of 1830 and about 45,000 Poles were banished from their homeland. In spite of the partitions the Poles kept their national feeling alive through music and language: Karol Kurpinski celebrated the national struggle through his operas and music and turned folk dances such as the polonaise and the mazurka into nationalist symbols. After the failure of the armed rebellion against Russian rule, members of the Polish clergy used language as a weapon of national resistance, using Polish for church gatherings and for all religious instruction, so that the use of Polish came to be seen as a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance.
items.ocr: The printed answer says ‘The idea of Polish position was not new’, evidently for ‘partition’; the sense is given in the answer above.

items.stem: How did nationalism develop through culture in Europe? Explain. or “Culture has played an important role in the development of nationalism in Europe during eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.” Support the statement with examples.
items.answer: Culture played an important role in creating the idea of the nation: art and poetry, stories and music helped express and shape nationalist feelings, and Romanticism in particular developed a distinctive form of nationalist sentiment. The Romantic artists turned away from the glorification of reason and science and focused on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings, seeking to create a sense of a shared collective heritage and a common cultural past as the basis of a nation. The German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder tried to popularise the true spirit of the nation through folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances, arguing that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people. The emphasis on vernacular language and the collection of local folklore served both to recover an ancient national spirit and to carry the modern nationalist message to large audiences who were mostly illiterate. In Poland, which had been partitioned by the great powers, national feelings were kept alive through music and language: the use of Polish came to be seen as a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance, and after the failure of an armed rebellion against Russian rule many members of the Polish clergy used language as a weapon of national resistance, using Polish for church gatherings and for all instruction. In France, likewise, a common language brought a collective identity among the French people.

items.stem: Discuss the characteristics of the nationalist movement in Greece.
items.answer: The Greeks began their war of independence in 1820 against the Ottoman Empire, and the awaited opportunity came in 1821 when Ali Pasha, the Turkish governor of Janina, quarrelled with the Sultan and went to war with him; Prince Hypsilanti was defeated in the battle at Moldavia by the Turks and the movement fizzled out for a short time. The war then developed into one of mutual extermination and was conducted on both sides with the utmost ferocity. For the first six years, from 1821 to 1828, the great powers did not intervene and the Greeks were left to their own efforts, Metternich being against giving help to revolutionaries. Nationalist feelings elsewhere in Europe were nevertheless strengthened by the Greek struggle: poets and artists such as Lord Byron, who organised funds and later went to fight and died of fever there, lauded Greece as the cradle of European civilisation and mobilised public opinion. To prevent independent action by Russia, Metternich induced France and Czar Nicholas I to join England in forcing an armistice on the Sultan. A conference was held in London in July 1827 and a joint note despatched to Turkey to grant autonomy, but the Sultan refused, whereupon the allied fleets of France and England destroyed the Turkish fleet at Navarino on 20 October 1827. By the Convention of London of 1832 the new kingdom of Greece was recognised and placed under the joint guarantee of the powers, and Prince Otto of Bavaria was chosen as its king. Greece thus afforded the first example of the victory of nationalism against the reactionary policy of the Congress of Vienna and struck a blow at Metternich’s system.

items.stem: Describe the process of unification of Germany.
items.answer: After 1848 nationalism in Europe moved away from its association with democracy and revolution, and nationalist sentiment was often mobilised by conservatives to promote state power and political domination. Germany was unified in this way. Thirty-nine German states had been grouped together in an organisation known as the German Confederation. In 1834 a customs union or Zollverein was established, which allowed free trade among its members and created a real national unity in economic matters. In May 1848 a large number of political associations voted for an all-German National Assembly at Frankfurt, which drafted a constitution for a German nation to be headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament; the crown was offered to the Prussian king but he rejected it, and the liberal initiative to nation-building failed. Thereafter the task of unification was taken over by Prussia and its chief minister Otto von Bismarck, who became the architect of modern Germany. Bismarck followed a policy of ‘blood and iron’ and carried out his plans with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy: within seven years three wars were fought, with Denmark, Austria and France, and all ended in Prussian victory. Finally, in January 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor, and the unification of Germany was complete.
